# What It Answers, What It Refuses, Who It Hands To

**Use it when:** an assistant is about to speak to customers in your client's name —
on the phone, in a chat, at the counter.
**It exists to stop:** the confident wrong answer about the thing that costs a family
money: a warranty, a tax rule, a legal status, a price.

> *Scope is a list, not a mood. "That one's for Yesenia" is a feature, not a failure.
> An instruction nudges; a gate stops. Write the three lists, test them with the
> questions people actually ask, and hand the person to a person.*

**Written in both of the client's languages, from the client's own instructions, tested
before a customer ever hears it.**

---

## What it answers

Only what is on this list. Every row names where the true answer lives, because an
assistant that answers from memory is guessing in the client's voice.

## What it refuses

The questions it must not answer even when it could. Each one has the refusal written
out, in both languages, naming the person it goes to. A refusal that names nobody is
a hang-up.

| Question type | Why it must refuse | Refusal — language 1 | Refusal — language 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
|  | money / legal / medical / a promise |  |  |
|  | money / legal / medical / a promise |  |  |
|  | money / legal / medical / a promise |  |  |

**The rule that is a gate, not an instruction:** ___ *(what stops the assistant before it
speaks — a word list, a topic check, a "not on the list" default — not a sentence in
its instructions asking it nicely)*

## The tested questions

Ask it the questions on the wall, the ones in the shoebox, the ones the nephew asked.
Include the ones that are almost on the list. Write down what it said, not what it
should have said.
